name: Insulin (bodybuilding use)

card.summary: Prescription diabetes hormone injected by some bodybuilders for muscle fullness; evidence for benefit is thin and hypoglycemia has been linked to deaths.
card.note: Risk of severe hypoglycemia, coma and death; prohibited for non-diabetic athletes.

quick.overview:
Insulin is the body's main anabolic hormone and a prescription medicine for diabetes. Some bodybuilders have reportedly injected it, often alongside steroids and growth hormone, hoping for more protein synthesis, glycogen storage and fuller muscles.

A reference article states the evidence supports these effects only in a small group of drug-naive individuals, and that whether insulin improves performance is unclear.
quick.mechanism: Insulin promotes glucose uptake in muscle and fat, glycogen storage, amino-acid uptake and protein synthesis, and slows protein and fat breakdown.
quick.risks: The main risk is hypoglycemia, which can progress to seizures, coma, brain damage or death. Insulin misuse has been mentioned as a possible factor in bodybuilder deaths. It is prescription-only in many countries and banned for non-diabetic athletes.

lead: Insulin is a peptide hormone that regulates blood glucose and is the main anabolic hormone of the body: it helps muscle and fat take in glucose, increases amino-acid uptake and protein synthesis, and slows liver glucose production and breakdown of fat and protein.[1] As a medicine it is used for diabetes.[2]

In bodybuilding circles, insulin is used for a physique goal: fuller, rounder muscles and more efficient 'nutrient partitioning', meaning that more of the calories eaten go to muscle glycogen and protein rather than fat. Some bodybuilders have reportedly injected regular insulin, often alongside anabolic steroids and growth hormone, in the belief that it increases protein synthesis, muscle glycogen storage, strength and stamina.[2] The look people are after is greater muscle size and fullness for a given amount of training and food.

The reference article on insulin as a medication states that these effects are supported only in a small group of drug-naive individuals, and notes that insulin misuse has been linked to some bodybuilder deaths.[2] On looksmax.org the topic appears in threads about stacking insulin with testosterone and growth hormone, and in threads about managing insulin resistance while using growth hormone or GLP-1 compounds.[3][4][5]

chain: Injected insulin raises glucose and amino-acid uptake into muscle
More glycogen and protein stored in muscle cells
Fuller, larger-looking muscles and better nutrient partitioning
angle.text: Bodybuilders who use insulin do so to make muscles look fuller and to drive more of the food they eat into muscle rather than fat. The mechanism follows insulin's normal role in glucose and amino-acid uptake, though the degree of benefit in healthy people is described as unclear in reference sources.

infobox: Prescription-only in the UK, EU and Canada
1921, Banting and Best, University of Toronto
Banned by the IOC for non-diabetic athletes since 1998

paras: Insulin was the first peptide hormone discovered, first isolated from dog pancreas in 1921 by Frederick Banting and Charles Best in John Macleod's laboratory in Toronto; Frederick Sanger sequenced it in 1951 and Dorothy Hodgkin determined its crystal structure in 1969.[1] It treats high blood glucose in diabetes and is prescription-only in Canada, the UK and the EU.[2]

sections.h: How it is meant to help muscle
paras: Physiologically, insulin signals muscle and fat cells to take up glucose, stores glycogen, increases amino-acid uptake and protein synthesis, and slows protein and fat breakdown.[1] Bodybuilders borrow this logic: an injection timed with carbohydrate-rich meals is meant to push glucose and amino acids into muscle, increasing glycogen storage and cell volume, which proponents associate with a fuller look.[2]

Because these actions mirror what insulin does naturally after a meal, advocates describe it as an extension of normal physiology. Reference sources note that the effect is supported only in a small group of drug-naive individuals and that overall performance benefit is unclear.[2]

According to the Wikipedia article on insulin as a medication, insulin was suggested as a performance aid around the 1998 Nagano Winter Olympics, and the International Olympic Committee banned its use by non-diabetic athletes that year.[2] The article says some bodybuilders reportedly inject regular insulin before sugary meals, with steroids and growth hormone.[2]

The article also cites allegations in the book Game of Shadows that baseball player Barry Bonds used insulin, and mentions insulin as a possible factor in the deaths of bodybuilders Ghent Wakefield and Rich Piana.[2]

The main risk is hypoglycemia, which can progress to confusion, seizures, coma, brain damage or death. Other effects include low blood potassium, allergic reactions in about 2 percent of people, and firm lumps from repeated injections at one site.[2] A 2008 report warned athletes combining insulin with growth hormone and IGF-I were exposing themselves to potential harm.[2]

On looksmax.org, insulin shows up in discussions about advanced 'roiding' pipelines. One thread asks why more people do not add insulin to testosterone, growth hormone and other compounds; replies there describe it as feared by many and as something few people use skillfully.[4] Another thread discusses combining growth hormone with compounds meant to reduce insulin resistance, with users debating metformin, berberine and SGLT2 inhibitors and their possible effects on mTOR and IGF-1.[3]

A further thread by a user who reports inherited insulin resistance lists fasting, chromium picolinate and other measures to improve insulin sensitivity, with replies suggesting metformin or retatrutide instead.[5] On T Nation, a participant answering a question about 'insulin manipulation' distinguished carb timing from injected insulin and said bodybuilders have injected it to improve nutrient partitioning.[6]

No studies found of insulin as a bodybuilding or performance aid in healthy non-diabetic athletes. The reference article states that whether insulin improves athletic performance is unclear.[2] Large bodies of research exist on insulin in diabetes care and on exercise and insulin sensitivity in people with type 2 diabetes, but these concern medical treatment rather than physique goals.[7]

timeline.event: Banting and Best isolate insulin in Toronto.[1]
The IOC bans insulin for non-diabetic athletes around the Nagano Winter Olympics.[2]
A report warns athletes combining insulin with GH and IGF-I risk harm.[2]

lore.intro: Insulin is discussed in bodybuilding and looksmaxxing forums under the nickname slin, as a nutrient-partitioning tool and as a factor to manage when using growth hormone.[3][4]

claims.claim: Insulin drives nutrients into muscle for fuller, faster-growing muscles
claims.believers: Users say it increases glycogen storage, muscle fullness and protein synthesis, and ask why more people do not add it to a stack.[4][6]
claims.experts: Effects are described as supported only in a small group of drug-naive individuals, and performance benefit is unclear.[2]

claims.claim: Insulin use can be managed safely with careful food intake
claims.believers: Some forum users say fear of it is overstated and that careful use avoids problems.[4]
claims.experts: Hypoglycemia can cause coma, brain damage or death, and misuse has been mentioned in bodybuilder deaths.[2]

claims.claim: Improving insulin sensitivity raises IGF-1 and supports growth
claims.believers: A forum guide argues fasting and supplements improve insulin sensitivity, which it links to higher IGF-1 and other hormones.[5]
claims.experts: No published studies in this wiki's sources test these specific measures for physique outcomes; the exercise literature examines insulin resistance in diabetes and obesity.[7]
